rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient centered in time and temperature to reveal the full retention spread and whether all 10 compounds elute within 42 min. The wide composition range and moderate slope maximize information for subsequent optimization.

All 10 compounds are already fully resolved, so the only way to improve CRF is to shorten the run without driving the minimum resolution below the target. A steeper gradient should pull the late peak earlier and test how much time can be saved while monitoring the close 5-8 cluster.

The 12 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the critical 6/7 pair, so a small increase in gradient time should recover that local resolution while likely keeping the run in the no-time-penalty region. This is a focused bracketing step between the successful 20 and over-steep 12 min methods.

Resolution improves steadily as tG increases, and the only problematic pair is still 6/7, so the next logical bracket is 16 min. This should test whether that pair reaches adequate separation while still likely avoiding any time penalty.

The optimum appears near tG 14–16 min, so now test temperature as a selectivity lever to improve the critical 6/7 separation without lengthening the run. A modest decrease to 35 C may differentially affect that pair and potentially raise the resolution term above the current best while keeping analysis time short.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so probe the opposite direction at the current best tG to see whether a small increase improves the crowded mid-cluster. This is the cleanest remaining one-factor test around the near-optimal 14 min method.

Temperature shifts changed selectivity substantially, so combine the more forgiving longer gradient with the cooler setting to see if the identities causing the 5/6 crowding at 35 C spread back out while preserving stronger separation of the original critical region. This explores a realistic interaction near the current optimum rather than moving farther in an unhelpful direction.

Keep the near-optimal gradient time and temperature, but raise phi0 to reduce early gradient strength at the column and probe selectivity in the crowded mid-elution cluster. This could reshuffle the critical pair without pushing the run into a time-penalty regime.

Increasing phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved both speed and the resolution term, so continue in the same direction at the current optimum tG and T. This tests whether the critical mid-cluster selectivity keeps improving before early compounds become too compressed.

The best region is now around phi0 0.10 with no time penalty, so adjust phi1 downward to reduce the overall gradient span and potentially decompress the critical 6/7 pair while keeping the run fast. The last peak is already comfortably early, so there is room to trade a little late elution strength for selectivity.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6/7 resolution while staying penalty-free, so continue one more step in that direction to see if the minimum pair reaches full target separation. The last peak is still early enough that a modest retention increase is acceptable.

CRF has reached the maximum, so this shot should only test whether an equally perfect score is possible with a shorter gradient. Keeping the now-optimal composition window and reducing tG probes whether run time can be cut without losing the critical 6/7 resolution.

You already have the maximum CRF, so use one confirmatory point around the optimum to map robustness. Extending to 16 min with the optimal composition window checks whether full resolution is maintained over a slightly broader operating space, which is useful if multiple methods can still score 1.000.

With the optimum pinned at 0.10/0.85/14/40, the most informative remaining nearby test is a slightly lower phi1 to see whether full resolution is retained or improved before any time penalty appears. This checks whether injection 11 is a broad maximum or a sharp optimum.

Test whether lowering phi0 while keeping the optimal phi1 restores or even improves selectivity in the critical mid-cluster without changing gradient span too drastically. This is the nearest unexplored composition adjustment around the winning method and helps define the local optimum.

You have mapped phi0 below the optimum with phi1 0.85; now test the symmetric higher phi0 side to confirm whether 0.10 is truly the local maximum. This completes the immediate composition neighborhood around the winning method.

A second maximum at phi0 0.15 suggests the optimum may extend to slightly stronger starting conditions, possibly with an even shorter last retention while keeping full resolution. Testing phi0 0.20 maps the fast edge of that 1.000-CRF plateau.

Since phi0 0.15 and phi1 0.85 gives a perfect score, the next useful nearby test is lowering phi1 one step at the same phi0 to see whether the 1.000 plateau extends to a slightly narrower gradient range. This probes whether you can keep full resolution while tuning around the second optimum.

Map the other side of the phi1 neighborhood around the second 1.000 point to see whether the perfect-score plateau also extends upward from phi1 0.85. This completes a compact local bracket around the fastest perfect method found so far.

Explore the faster corner combining higher phi0 with higher phi1 to see whether selectivity loss at phi0 0.20 can be offset by the broader gradient span. This is a final local boundary check around the 1.000-CRF plateau.

Complete the remaining nearby corner around the high-phi0 region to define the boundary of the perfect-score zone. This will show whether stronger starting solvent can still maintain full resolution if the final strength is reduced.

The 1.000 region appears to extend to higher phi0 when phi1 is 0.80, so push one more step to locate the upper edge of that plateau. This may identify the fastest still-perfect composition or show where early compression starts to hurt the critical pair.

The failure at phi0 0.25 with phi1 0.80 came from excessive early compression, so increase phi1 one step to broaden the gradient span and see if the early pair re-separates while retaining the otherwise favorable pattern. This pinpoints whether the upper phi0 limit depends mainly on gradient range.

The perfect-score region includes phi0 0.20 with phi1 0.80, so lowering phi1 one step tests the lower boundary of that plateau while avoiding the clearly bad phi0 0.25 space. This is a targeted edge check with low risk of missing all compounds.

For the final shot, test whether the early-pair failure at phi0 0.25 can be rescued by the widest remaining gradient span; if not, it cleanly confirms phi0 0.25 is beyond the useful boundary. All evidence still supports the 1.000-CRF plateau around phi0 0.10-0.20 and phi1 0.80-0.85.
